title: 1  Project 1 — CATA vs. RATA on instant coffee

2 Research question
Does adding intensity ratings (RATA) improve product discrimination compared with plain CATA?
Sub-questions that each group must answer:

section: 8.2 CATA: Cochran’s Q test per attribute
text:
8.2 CATA: Cochran’s Q test per attribute
Cochran’s Q tests whether the proportion of panelists ticking an attribute differs across products. It is the CATA equivalent of a one-way repeated-measures ANOVA on binary data.

cochran_q <- function(y, block, treat) {
  m  <- tapply(y, list(block, treat), sum)          # blocks x treatments, 0/1
  k  <- ncol(m); Cj <- colSums(m); Ri <- rowSums(m); N <- sum(m)
  Q  <- (k - 1) * (k * sum(Cj^2) - N^2) / (k * N - sum(Ri^2))
  c(Q = Q, df = k - 1, p = pchisq(Q, k - 1, lower.tail = FALSE))
}

cata_q <- t(sapply(attrs, function(a) cochran_q(cata[[a]], cata$panelist, cata$sample)))
cata_q <- data.frame(attribute = attrs, round(cata_q, 4))
cata_q$significant <- cata_q$p < 0.05
cata_q

8.3 CATA: correspondence analysis
Run CA only on the attributes that discriminate (significant Cochran’s Q).

sig_cata <- cata_q$attribute[cata_q$significant]
ca_cata  <- CA(cata_freq[, sig_cata], graph = FALSE)
round(ca_cata$eig[1:3, ], 1)

      eigenvalue percentage of variance cumulative percentage of variance
dim 1        0.5                   62.2                              62.2
dim 2        0.1                   17.6                              79.8
dim 3        0.1                    9.7                              89.5

ca_rows <- data.frame(ca_cata$row$coord[, 1:2], label = rownames(cata_freq), type = "Sample")
ca_cols <- data.frame(ca_cata$col$coord[, 1:2], label = sig_cata,           type = "Attribute")
ggplot(rbind(ca_rows, ca_cols), aes(Dim.1, Dim.2, colour = type, label = label)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, lty = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point() + geom_text_repel(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "CATA - correspondence analysis",
       x = sprintf("Dim 1 (%.1f%%)", ca_cata$eig[1, 2]),
       y = sprintf("Dim 2 (%.1f%%)", ca_cata$eig[2, 2])) +
  theme_minimal()

title: 1  Project 1 — CATA vs. RATA on instant coffee
text:
8.4 RATA: two-way ANOVA per attribute
Model per attribute: score ~ sample + panelist (panelist as a block). Then Tukey HSD to count discriminated pairs.

rata_aov <- t(sapply(attrs, function(a) {
  fit <- aov(as.formula(paste(a, "~ sample + panelist")), data = rata)
  s   <- summary(fit)[[1]]
  tk  <- TukeyHSD(fit, "sample")$sample
  c(F = s["sample", "F value"], p = s["sample", "Pr(>F)"],
    pairs_diff = sum(tk[, "p adj"] < 0.05))
}))
rata_aov <- data.frame(attribute = attrs, round(rata_aov, 4))
rata_aov$significant <- rata_aov$p < 0.05
rata_aov

title: 1  Project 1 — CATA vs. RATA on instant coffee
text:
8.6 Comparing the two methods

8.6.1 Similarity of the product maps: RV coefficient
Both maps must have the products in the same row order.

X <- ca_cata$row$coord[codes, 1:2]
Y <- pca_rata$ind$coord[codes, 1:2]
rv <- coeffRV(X, Y)
rv[c("rv", "rvstd", "p.value")]

$rv
[1] 0.9191706

$rvstd
[1] 4.36977

$p.value
[1] 0.002798794




8.6.2 Discrimination: how many product pairs does each method separate?
For CATA, a pair of products is “discriminated” on an attribute if McNemar’s test is significant. For RATA, we already have Tukey HSD.

pairs <- combn(levels(cata$sample), 2)
cata_pairs <- sapply(sig_cata, function(a) {
  sum(apply(pairs, 2, function(pr) {
    x <- cata[cata$sample == pr[1], c("panelist", a)]
    y <- cata[cata$sample == pr[2], c("panelist", a)]
    m <- merge(x, y, by = "panelist")
    tab <- table(factor(m[[2]], 0:1), factor(m[[3]], 0:1))
    if (tab[1, 2] + tab[2, 1] == 0) return(FALSE)
    mcnemar.test(tab)$p.value < 0.05
  }))
})
data.frame(attribute = attrs,
           CATA_pairs = ifelse(attrs %in% sig_cata, cata_pairs[attrs], 0),
           RATA_pairs = rata_aov$pairs_diff)


  



Look in particular at the near-duplicate pair 219 vs. 573: neither method should separate them strongly. If one method does, it may be picking up noise.


8.6.3 Summary table for the poster

data.frame(
  Criterion = c("Discriminating attributes (p < 0.05)",
                "Variance explained, Dim 1 + 2 (%)",
                "Discriminated product pairs (sum over attributes)",
                "RV between maps (p-value)"),
  CATA = c(length(sig_cata),
           round(ca_cata$eig[2, 3], 1),
           sum(cata_pairs),
           sprintf("%.2f (p = %.3f)", rv$rv, rv$p.value)),
  RATA = c(length(sig_rata),
           round(pca_rata$eig[2, 3], 1),
           sum(rata_aov$pairs_diff),
           ""))

title: 2  Project 2 — Napping vs. Polarized Sensory Positioning (PSP) on ready-to-drink teas
text:
3 Research question
Does rating samples against fixed reference poles (PSP) give a product map similar to free placement on a sheet (Napping)?
Sub-questions:
Design. Within-subjects: the same ~40 untrained consumers do both methods, in counterbalanced order (half Napping first, half PSP first), with a break in between. 10 ready-to-drink teas, 3-digit codes. For PSP, 3 of the 10 teas are served as labelled poles (Pole A, B, C); all 10 teas, including the 3 pole teas, are also served blind as test samples.

text:
9.1 Napping: multiple factor analysis (MFA)
Each panelist is a group of 2 unstandardised continuous variables (type = "c"). MFA balances the panelists so that nobody dominates because they used a larger part of the sheet.

n_pan <- ncol(nap_mat) / 2
mfa <- MFA(nap_mat, group = rep(2, n_pan), type = rep("c", n_pan),
           name.group = paste0("P", 1:n_pan), graph = FALSE)
round(mfa$eig[1:4, ], 1)

       eigenvalue percentage of variance cumulative percentage of variance
comp 1       31.3                   59.9                              59.9
comp 2       11.0                   21.0                              81.0
comp 3        2.1                    3.9                              84.9
comp 4        1.8                    3.5                              88.5


Placing the words on the map. Each word is placed at the weighted average position of the teas it was used for (weights = how often it was cited for each tea). A word used only for the jasmine teas sits among the jasmine teas; a word used for many different teas ends up near the centre, which tells you it does not discriminate.

prod_xy  <- mfa$ind$coord[rownames(word_tab), 1:2]
word_xy  <- t(as.matrix(word_tab)) %*% prod_xy / colSums(word_tab)
word_coord <- data.frame(word_xy, word = colnames(word_tab), n = colSums(word_tab))
word_coord[order(-word_coord$n), ]


  




nap_coord <- data.frame(mfa$ind$coord[, 1:2], code = rownames(nap_mat))
ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, lty = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(data = nap_coord, aes(Dim.1, Dim.2), size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(data = nap_coord, aes(Dim.1, Dim.2, label = code)) +
  geom_text_repel(data = word_coord, aes(Dim.1, Dim.2, label = word, size = n),
                  max.overlaps = Inf, colour = "steelblue", fontface = "italic",
                  show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_size(range = c(3, 5)) +
  labs(title = "Napping - MFA product map with descriptors",
       subtitle = "Words placed at the weighted average of the teas they describe; larger = cited more often",
       x = sprintf("Dim 1 (%.1f%%)", mfa$eig[1, 2]),
       y = sprintf("Dim 2 (%.1f%%)", mfa$eig[2, 2])) +
  theme_minimal()








Panelist plot — panelists close to the Dim 1 axis separated teas mainly on Dim 1, and so on. Panelists near the origin did not reproduce the consensus.

  rename(panelist = `Panelist ID`, code = `Sample code`,

         B = `How different is this sample from Pole B?`,
         C = `How different is this sample from Pole C?`)
poles <- c(A = "274", B = "605", C = "721")       # replace with your pole codes

psp %>% filter(code %in% poles) %>%
  group_by(code) %>% summarise(across(c(A, B, C), mean)) %>%
  mutate(own_pole = names(poles)[match(code, poles)])

title: 2  Project 2 — Napping vs. Polarized Sensory Positioning (PSP) on ready-to-drink teas
text:
9.3 PSP: product map
Each panelist describes each product by its 3 distances to the poles. As in Napping, we build a product × (panelist × pole) matrix and run MFA with each panelist as a group of 3 variables. This keeps the two analyses parallel.

psp_mat <- psp %>%
  pivot_longer(c(A, B, C), names_to = "pole", values_to = "d") %>%
  mutate(col = paste0("P", panelist, "_", pole)) %>%
  select(code, col, d) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = col, values_from = d) %>%
  arrange(code) %>% tibble::column_to_rownames("code")

n_psp <- ncol(psp_mat) / 3
mfa_psp <- MFA(psp_mat, group = rep(3, n_psp), type = rep("c", n_psp),
               name.group = paste0("P", 1:n_psp), graph = FALSE)
round(mfa_psp$eig[1:3, ], 1)

       eigenvalue percentage of variance cumulative percentage of variance
comp 1       37.3                   60.8                              60.8
comp 2       16.1                   26.3                              87.0
comp 3        2.3                    3.7                              90.8

psp_coord <- data.frame(mfa_psp$ind$coord[, 1:2], code = rownames(psp_mat),
                        pole = ifelse(rownames(psp_mat) %in% poles, "pole", "test"))
ggplot(psp_coord, aes(Dim.1, Dim.2, label = code, colour = pole)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, lty = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 3) + geom_text_repel(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "PSP - MFA product map",
       x = sprintf("Dim 1 (%.1f%%)", mfa_psp$eig[1, 2]),
       y = sprintf("Dim 2 (%.1f%%)", mfa_psp$eig[2, 2])) +
  theme_minimal()








Alternative used in Teillet et al. (2010): average the PSP ratings to a product × pole table and run a PCA, or compute product-to-product distances and use classical MDS (cmdscale()). Try one and check that the map is similar.

text:
9.4 Comparing the two methods

9.4.1 RV coefficient between the maps

X  <- mfa$ind$coord[codes, 1:2]
Y  <- mfa_psp$ind$coord[codes, 1:2]
rv <- coeffRV(X, Y)
rv[c("rv", "rvstd", "p.value")]

$rv
[1] 0.9729596

$rvstd
[1] 6.144577

$p.value
[1] 0.0001680678




9.4.2 Procrustes: superimpose the two maps
The PSP map is rotated, scaled and (if needed) mirrored to best match the Napping map. Long arrows = teas positioned differently by the two methods.

procrustes <- function(X, Y) {                    # rotate/scale Y onto X
  Xc <- scale(X, scale = FALSE); Yc <- scale(Y, scale = FALSE)
  s  <- svd(t(Yc) %*% Xc); R <- s$u %*% t(s$v)
  b  <- sum(s$d) / sum(Yc^2)
  b * Yc %*% R
}
Xc <- scale(X, scale = FALSE)
Yp <- procrustes(X, Y)
df <- data.frame(code = codes, xn = Xc[, 1], yn = Xc[, 2], xp = Yp[, 1], yp = Yp[, 2])
ggplot(df) +
  geom_segment(aes(xn, yn, xend = xp, yend = yp), colour = "grey50",
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(.15, "cm"))) +
  geom_point(aes(xn, yn, colour = "Napping"), size = 3) +
  geom_point(aes(xp, yp, colour = "PSP (rotated)"), size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(xn, yn, label = code)) +
  labs(title = "Procrustes overlay of Napping and PSP maps", x = "Dim 1", y = "Dim 2",
       colour = NULL) + theme_minimal()

  inner_join(psp_ease %>% select(panelist = `Panelist ID`, PSP = `How easy was the PSP task?`),
             by = "panelist")

title: 3  Project 3 — Free sorting vs. CATA on snack chips
text:
4 Research question
Does a holistic method (free sorting) reveal the same product groupings as an attribute-based method (CATA), and which method do consumers find easier?
Sub-questions:
Design. Within-subjects, counterbalanced: the same ~50 untrained consumers do both tasks in one session (half sort first, half CATA first), with a break and fresh samples in between. 9 chips (e.g., keripik tempe, cassava, potato and banana chips in several flavours), 3-digit codes.

text:
10.1 Sorting: multiple correspondence analysis (MCA)
Treating each panelist’s partition as a categorical variable and running MCA is the approach of the fast() function in SensoMineR.

mca <- MCA(sort_mat, graph = FALSE)
round(mca$eig[1:4, ], 1)

      eigenvalue percentage of variance cumulative percentage of variance
dim 1        0.7                   30.6                              30.6
dim 2        0.6                   24.4                              55.0
dim 3        0.3                   11.4                              66.4
dim 4        0.3                   10.9                              77.2


Each word is placed at the weighted average position of the products it was used for (weights = number of citations). Words used for one type of chip sit next to those chips; words used for many chips end up near the centre.

sort_coord <- data.frame(mca$ind$coord[, 1:2], code = codes)
word_xy    <- t(as.matrix(sort_words)) %*% mca$ind$coord[rownames(sort_words), 1:2] /
              colSums(sort_words)
word_coord <- data.frame(word_xy, word = colnames(sort_words), n = colSums(sort_words),
                         in_cata = colnames(sort_words) %in% tolower(terms))

ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, lty = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(data = sort_coord, aes(Dim.1, Dim.2), size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(data = sort_coord, aes(Dim.1, Dim.2, label = code), fontface = "bold") +
  geom_text_repel(data = word_coord, aes(Dim.1, Dim.2, label = word, size = n, colour = in_cata),
                  fontface = "italic", max.overlaps = Inf) +
  scale_size(range = c(3, 5), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "steelblue", `FALSE` = "darkorange"),
                      labels = c(`TRUE` = "in CATA list", `FALSE` = "not in CATA list"),
                      name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Free sorting - MCA product map with group descriptors",
       subtitle = "Words placed at the weighted average of the products they describe",
       x = sprintf("Dim 1 (%.1f%%)", mca$eig[1, 2]),

10.3 CATA: Cochran’s Q and correspondence analysis

cochran_q <- function(y, block, treat) {
  m  <- tapply(y, list(block, treat), sum)
  k  <- ncol(m); Cj <- colSums(m); Ri <- rowSums(m); N <- sum(m)
  Q  <- (k - 1) * (k * sum(Cj^2) - N^2) / (k * N - sum(Ri^2))
  c(Q = Q, p = pchisq(Q, k - 1, lower.tail = FALSE))
}
cata_q <- data.frame(term = terms,
                     t(sapply(terms, function(a) cochran_q(cata[[a]], cata$panelist, cata$sample))))
cata_q$significant <- cata_q$p < 0.05
cata_q

  tibble::column_to_rownames("sample") %>% as.matrix()

ca  <- CA(cata_freq[, sig], graph = FALSE)

10.4.2 Do the clusters agree?
Cross-tabulate the clusters from both methods. The adjusted Rand index (ARI) summarises agreement between two partitions: 1 = identical, 0 = no better than chance.

table(sorting = sort_clusters, CATA = cata_clusters[names(sort_clusters)])

ari <- function(a, b) {
  tab <- table(a, b); n <- sum(tab)
  sc  <- sum(choose(tab, 2)); sa <- sum(choose(rowSums(tab), 2)); sb <- sum(choose(colSums(tab), 2))
  exp <- sa * sb / choose(n, 2)
  (sc - exp) / ((sa + sb) / 2 - exp)
}

text:
11.3 JAR: penalty analysis
For each sample × attribute:

% of consumers in the Too low and Too high groups;
mean drop = mean liking of the JAR group − mean liking of the Too low (or Too high) group;
weighted penalty = mean drop × proportion.

Common decision rule: a problem is actionable when ≥ 20% of consumers are in the non-JAR group and the mean drop is ≥ 1 point on the 9-point scale.

penalty <- jar_long %>%
  group_by(sample, attribute) %>%
  mutate(jar_mean = mean(liking[category == "JAR"]), n_total = n()) %>%
  filter(category != "JAR") %>%
  group_by(sample, attribute, category) %>%
  summarise(pct = 100 * n() / first(n_total), n = n(),
            mean_drop = first(jar_mean) - mean(liking), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(weighted_penalty = mean_drop * pct / 100,
         actionable = pct >= 20 & mean_drop >= 1 & n >= 5)
penalty %>% arrange(desc(weighted_penalty)) %>% print(n = 12)

section: 11.4 CATA + ideal: penalty analysis (Ares et al., 2014)
text:
11.4 CATA + ideal: penalty analysis (Ares et al., 2014)
For each term, every consumer × sample falls in one of four cells:









Ideal: yes
Ideal: no




Product: yes
P(yes) I(yes) — OK
P(yes) I(no) — term present but should not be


Product: no
P(no) I(yes) — term missing but should be there
P(no) I(no) — OK




“Must have” penalty = liking[P yes, I yes] − liking[P no, I yes]
“Must not have” penalty = liking[P no, I no] − liking[P yes, I no]

Each penalty is tested with a t-test. A term matters when the penalty is significant and affects ≥ 20% of consumers.

cata_pen <- bind_rows(lapply(terms, function(a) {
  d  <- cata_long %>% filter(term == a)
  ok_yes  <- d$liking[d$product == 1 & d$ideal == 1]
  miss    <- d$liking[d$product == 0 & d$ideal == 1]
  ok_no   <- d$liking[d$product == 0 & d$ideal == 0]
  extra   <- d$liking[d$product == 1 & d$ideal == 0]
  tt <- function(x, y) if (length(x) > 2 && length(y) > 2) t.test(x, y)$p.value else NA
  data.frame(term = a,
             type = c("Missing (must have)", "Present (must not have)"),
             pct  = 100 * c(length(miss), length(extra)) / nrow(d),
             mean_drop = c(mean(ok_yes) - mean(miss), mean(ok_no) - mean(extra)),
             p = c(tt(ok_yes, miss), tt(ok_no, extra)))
}))
cata_pen <- cata_pen %>%
  mutate(weighted_penalty = mean_drop * pct / 100,
         actionable = !is.na(p) & p < 0.05 & pct >= 20)
cata_pen %>% arrange(desc(weighted_penalty)) %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(., 3)))


  




ggplot(cata_pen %>% filter(!is.na(mean_drop)),
       aes(pct, mean_drop, colour = actionable, shape = type)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 20, xmax = Inf, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, alpha = .08, fill = "red") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") + geom_vline(xintercept = 20, lty = 2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) + geom_text_repel(aes(label = term), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#E45756", `FALSE` = "grey50")) +
  labs(title = "CATA-ideal penalty analysis (all samples pooled)",
       x = "% of consumer x sample cases", y = "Mean drop in liking", shape = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

11.5 CATA + ideal: where does each sample deviate from the ideal?
For the actionable terms, the % of consumers whose description of a sample differs from their ideal tells you which samples to change.

act <- cata_pen %>% filter(actionable)
cata_by_sample <- cata_long %>%
  inner_join(act %>% select(term, type), by = "term") %>%
  group_by(sample, term, type) %>%
  summarise(pct_deviating = 100 * mean(
              ifelse(type == "Missing (must have)", product == 0 & ideal == 1,
                     product == 1 & ideal == 0)), .groups = "drop")
cata_by_sample %>%
  mutate(label = paste0(term, ifelse(type == "Missing (must have)", " (missing)", " (present)"))) %>%
  select(sample, label, pct_deviating) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = label, values_from = pct_deviating) %>%
  mutate(across(-sample, ~ round(., 0)))
